newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Dlr near 31-month high vs mark after US data.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Dlr near 31-month high vs mark after US data.

text.p: The dollar zoomed to a near 31-month high against the mark on Friday after better- than-expected U.S. trade data gave it the ammunition to breach stiff resistance levels.
"It was the smaller-than-expected U.S. trade deficit data that gave the dollar a boost," said Craig Shute, fixed income analyst at Bear Stearns.

The market had spent the morning wrestling with tough technical resistance at 1.6050-60 marks, marking time before key U.S. economic data later in the day and a holiday in the United States on Monday.

The U.S. trade deficit for November was $8.40 billion, widening from $8.01 billion in the previous month. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast on average a deficit of 9.8 billion dollars for November.
The dollar sailed through technical barriers to the day's high of 1.6125 marks after the trade figures, up from 1.5957 at the European close on Thursday.
At 1600 GMT it was at 1.6110 marks and 117.07 yen, compared with 1.5958 and 116.52 in late European trade on Thursday.
The barrier of 1.6050-60 marks represented the 61.8 percent Fibonacci retracement of the drop from 1.7686 in February 1994 to the record low at 1.3430 in March 1995.
The dollar also jumped to a high of 117.25 yen on the trade data, which showed the U.S. trade deficit with Japan had narrowed 12.9 percent to $4.32 billion in November.
Analysts said figures pointing to a robust U.S. economy would be likely to give the dollar another boost.

"That (stronger than expected data) would add to speculation of a Fed tightening, and that on the whole is cautiously positive for the dollar, so long as there's a belief that the actual tightening won't be overly aggressive," said Jeremy Hawkins, chief European economist at BankAmerica.

Industrial production data for December, also released on Friday, were also robust. Industrial production rose 0.8 percent from the previous month, above economists expectations for a rise of 0.6 percent.
Capacity utilisation was at 83.8 percent, in line with expectations.
Apart from wariness of Japanese government authorities about a stronger dollar, fundamentally there was little on the horizon to quash dollar bullishness.

"There isn't an awful lot standing in its way... The markets have got the view now that if they don't run into official resistance, they're just going to take it higher," said Robin Marshall, chief economist at Chase Investment Bank.
The incentive for a strong dollar/mark was coming from the German side as much as from the U.S., analysts said, citing mark weakness across the board and gloomy news about the German economy.

The mark fell against other European currencies in European trade, sinking to a new 52-month low against the Norwegian crown and sterling. It also hit new lows in the current move down against the lira and the escudo.
